Portuguese & English review Portuguese- Tarantino nunca conseguiu chegar a fazer um bom western nas suas tentativas, acaba por não haver uma compreensão de que o seu género de filmar quer realmente chegar ao com Django Unchained e The Hateful Eight, não há realmente uma correlação ou sensatez na utilização do Spaghetti Western. ​O grande problema destas tentativas de Tarantino, tanto em Django Unchained (2012) de forma mais gritante, como em The Hateful Eight, é que o realizador parece acreditar que fazer um Spaghetti Western se resume a decalcar a banda sonora de Ennio Morricone, usar lentes anamórficas de 70mm, filmar planos de pormenor de armas a saírem do coldre e carregar na violência hiperbolizada. Há uma total ausência de correlação e sensatez na utilização do género. O Spaghetti Western original aquele de Sergio Leone, Sergio Corbucci ou Giulio Questi nunca foi apenas sobre o estilo ou sobre "gajos fixes a disparar" era um cinema de urgência, seco, operático, que nascia de uma profunda desilusão do pós-guerra europeu, onde a violência era o reflexo de um mundo desprovido de Deus, de leis e de pátria, onde o silêncio e o deserto falavam mais do que os diálogos. ​Tarantino faz exatamente o oposto: ele sufoca o Western com o seu próprio estilo de filmar, transformando o que deveria ser um género visceral num exercício de autocomplacência verbal. The Hateful Eight falha na raiz porque renega o espaço do Western para se fechar numa peça de teatro filmada, claustrofóbica e tagarela, onde a dinâmica de "quem é quem" dentro duma cabana de neve se assemelha mais a um mistério de Agatha Christie reescrito com palavrões do que à crueza mítica de um clássico da fronteira. As personagens não são anti-heróis ambíguos e fascinantes na linha dos clássicos são apenas bonecos de cartão-canelado, odiosos e cínicos por decreto, criados para debitar monólogos intermináveis que tentam soar profundos mas que apenas revelam um realizador refém do seu próprio maneirismo. ​Não há sensatez moral na violência de Tarantino aqui. Enquanto no Spaghetti Western a brutalidade era trágica, suja e pesada, em The Hateful Eight ela torna-se meramente recreativa, um espetáculo gore gratuito e niilista que perde toda a força catártica. Ao tentar fundir a herança política da Guerra Civil Americana com o cinismo do Western europeu, Tarantino acaba por não chegar a lado nenhum. O filme arrasta-se num ritmo indulgente de três horas, onde a tensão nunca se traduz em peso dramático real, apenas numa contagem de corpos previsível. É o cinema transformado num parque de diversões temático para o próprio realizador, provando que, para se fazer um bom Western, não basta ter em arquivo uma gigantesca coleção de referências; é preciso compreender a mecânica do silêncio, a solidão do horizonte e a gravidade de um corpo que tomba no chão. Ainda um pouco melhor que Django Unchained. English- Tarantino never managed to make a good Western in his attempts, ultimately failing to understand what his genre of filmmaking really wants to achieve with Django Unchained and The Hateful Eight; there's really no correlation or common sense in the use of the Spaghetti Western. The big problem with Tarantino's attempts, both in Django Unchained (2012), most glaringly, and in The Hateful Eight, is that the director seems to believe that making a Spaghetti Western boils down to using Ennio Morricone's soundtrack, employing 70mm anamorphic lenses, filming close-ups of guns being drawn from holsters, and relying heavily on hyperbolized violence. There is a total lack of correlation and wisdom in the use of the genre. The original Spaghetti Western, the one by Sergio Leone, Sergio Corbucci, or Giulio Questi, was never just about style or "nice guys shooting." It was a cinema of urgency, dry, operatic, born from a profound disillusionment with postwar Europe, where violence reflected a world devoid of God, laws, and homeland, where silence and the desert spoke louder than dialogue. Tarantino does the exact opposite: he suffocates the Western with his own filming style, transforming what should be a visceral genre into an exercise in verbal self-indulgence. The Hateful Eight fails at its core because it rejects the space of the Western to enclose itself in a filmed, claustrophobic, and chatty play, where the "who's who" dynamic inside a snow cabin resembles more an Agatha Christie mystery rewritten with profanity than the mythical rawness of a frontier classic. The characters are not ambiguous and fascinating anti-heroes in the vein of the classics; they are merely corrugated cardboard puppets, hateful and cynical by decree, created to deliver endless monologues that attempt to sound profound but only reveal a director held hostage by his own mannerisms. There is no moral sense in Tarantino's violence here. While in the Spaghetti Western the brutality was tragic, dirty, and heavy, in The Hateful Eight it becomes merely recreational, a gratuitous and nihilistic gore spectacle that loses all cathartic force. In trying to merge the political legacy of the American Civil War with the cynicism of the European Western, Tarantino ends up getting nowhere. The film drags on at an indulgent three-hour pace, where the tension never translates into real dramatic weight, just a predictable body count. It is cinema transformed into a theme park for the director himself, proving that, to make a good Western, it is not enough to have a gigantic collection of references in the archives; It's necessary to understand the mechanics of silence, the solitude of the horizon, and the gravity of a body falling to the ground. Still a little better than Django Unchained.

Samuel L Jackson and Walton Goggins deliver great performances, the scope cinematography is excellent and Ennio Morricone’s music from The Thing and others is used to great effect. But I didn’t like this any more than the last time I saw it, which was in the cinema on release. It doesn’t hold together like other Tarantino movies for me, and the stylistic choices (particularly the director’s deliberately intrusive voiceover after the intermission) often come across as smug rather than clever. The worst thing is the way it wears its misogyny on its sleeve, not helped by the presence of the Weinstein name and logo all over the credits. It’s inspired by classic westerns of the 60s and 70s that have clearly racist and misogynistic moments… but those films were made over 50 years ago. This is from 2015 (although that’s a lifetime away in some respects). The use of slur words is extreme, even for Tarantino, and the final scene so grotesque that it overshadows anything good that came before. I don’t know anymore if it’s okay to admire the craft of a film if you find so much of the content repulsive.

Bon j'avoue que ce film de notre cher Quentin Tarantino s'annonçait sympa avec notamment un retour aux sources pour Morricone qui a fini par avoir son Oscar via ce film. Cependant le film joue avec brillo sur les dialogues qui restent le point fort du réalisateur et qui révèlent le type de personnage à qui l'on a affaire avec en prime un twist plutôt simple mais qui est mal foutu selon moi. Et que dire du visuel juste magnifique et Tarantinesque si ce terme existe bel et bien. Malheureusement je trouve que le film est peut-être mal construit et structuré le rendant plutôt ennuyant car au final il ne se passe pas grand chose d'intéressant mis à part cette histoire de lettre de Abraham Lincoln que possède le personnage de Samuel L Jackson. Apparently unpopular opinion, but I really didn't like this movie. This movie truly felt like it was six hours long. It was a real chore to sit through. I don't mind dialogue driven films, but the dialogue has to actually be interesting and compelling. It should be additive and purposeful. But here it was mundane and repetitive. It felt like there were multiple conversations that just kept repeating themselves just with different people. Most of these conversations served no real purpose. I'd say a lot of scenes in general even beyond just the dialogue felt pointless. Every scene felt like it was lasting too long. I really did not need to see 10 different scenes of them nailing the door shut. I get it, the door is broken. Nor did I need to see the origin story for said broken door. I really didn't care how it broke. I get what the film was trying to do. It was trying to slowly build tension between everyone until it boils over and turns into a big brawl by the end. But the problem is I never felt this tension. First of all because I never cared about a single character in this movie. There was not a single person I was rooting for. But also because everything was so drawn out any tension that is built up runs out of steam and lost the tension for me because I just wanted them to get on with it. Characters choices just didn't often make sense either. But they had to do things to make it as drawn out as humanly possible. The film was well acted though, I would acknowledge that, at least from most people. Samuel L Jackson does a great job in particular. He probably has the best lines. The ones that actually feel like they mattered. So I don't think the film is without merit whatsoever. But there wasn't a moment in the film where I just was ready for the film to be over already.

Okay, unfortunately, here we have yet another Tarantino Film that just didn't really impress me. But this time I want to start with the positives, because just like with his other Films, this one isn’t really bad, it’s just not my cup of tea and less interesting to me. So what do I like about it? I think the visuals are great; snowy Wyoming is beautiful, and I especially liked the shots from the beginning. Later on in the cabin, there isn’t quite as much to appreciate visually, but that’s okay. Next, I really like the soundtrack, I especially loved “Apple Blossom,” which went straight into my playlist. Plus, I thought the characters’ outfits were really, really cool. They were all dressed in that Western look, of course, but they all still looked different and unique in their own way, which I thought was really great. I also thought a lot of the ideas and characters were really strong, like how they divided the room between Southerners and Northerners, etc. The accents of the voice actors in the original version were great, too. The characters were all pretty good, too, I especially liked Major Marquis and the sheriff; they were authentic and well-written, and the rest were fine as well. Now let’s get to what I didn’t find that exciting and what didn’t really grab me. And that’s the whole story and the plot. It wasn’t bad by any means, but unfortunately, first of all, the story didn’t really interest me, and second, it wasn’t gripping or significant. Unfortunately, I caught myself several times wishing the Film would end soon, it dragged on incredibly. Maybe the dialogue was great, like in almost all of Tarantino’s Films, but I think the problem here is that when you rely solely on dialogue, the rest of the Film suffers, which was the case here. I have absolutely no idea about things like camera work, etc., so I don’t have much to say on that front, at least, I didn’t notice anything negative in that regard. So, to sum it up, this was probably a good Film, but unfortunately, it wasn’t my cup of tea at all, since it didn’t really interest me and dragged on quite a bit around the middle.

QT’s There Will Be Blood, a violent, sadistic Western that amounts to something like an origin myth. It is easily his most alienating, least likable movie, and it competes with Django Unchained as his worst. It is baggy, self-indulgent, undisciplined filmmaking. You can sense the willful perversity behind it: It’s almost like a self-imposed challenge — how to make a 2-hour, 45-minute epic in the confines of a single location. (He fails his own challenge.) But despite my reservations, the go-for-broke, don’t-give-a-shit folly of it all earns respect, if not admiration. He knows exactly what he’s doing. I think he knows that there is not a single likable person here (see the title), that the violence is as over-the-top as it’s been in any of his movies, and that he’s pushing the limits of audience patience. He thinks his voice, his talent, his virtuosity, the power of his message, and his audience’s loyalty will carry him through. They don’t, not all the way at least.

Le risque de développer un style de mise en scène est à la longue de s'enfermer dedans et d'en être prisonnier. Peut être que certains esprits plus fermés et ayant une très grande confiance en eux sont moins propices à la remise en question et aux changements propres à la curiosité, ce qui en découle une certaine stagnation quel que soit ce que l'on fait. Ça fait 30 ans que Tarantino répète les mêmes schémas qu'ils narratifs ou dans sa mise en scène. Déjà très marqués dès Pulp fiction, j'ai l'impression que l'on atteint le plus haut dans Kill Bill. Depuis j'ai cette sensation de plus en plus présente dès Inglorious Bastard de revoir les mêmes mécaniques avec seul un décors en toile de fond qui changeait. Si dans ce dernier, cela passait encore, cette impression dérangeante s'est accentuée dans Jango. Ici avec Hateful Eight, cela en est presque une caricature de son propre style, tout devient trop un Déjà Vu et même les dialogues, souvent riches chez Tarantino sont un peu en deçà. Le film demeure agréable et sympathique mais je certaine lassitude l'emporte. Il a néanmoins rompu avec ce style avec Once upon a Time in Hollywood, ce que j'avais apprécié, même si il s'est rappelé à lui même dans les 15 dernieres minutes.

Wow, this movie is something else. I honestly didn't know what to expect going into The Hateful Eight, but I ended up really enjoying it. The movie is pretty slow at first, but I think that's what makes it work. Most of it takes place inside one cabin, with a bunch of strangers who don't trust each other. As the movie goes on, you start questioning everyone and wondering who's actually telling the truth. The line “I’m gonna get you” really fits the feeling of the movie because you constantly feel like someone is about to turn on someone else. The dialogue is probably my favorite part. There isn't always a lot happening, but the conversations are so interesting that I didn't really mind. Tarantino can make people sitting around a table talking feel more intense than an action scene. The characters are constantly trying to figure each other out, and that paranoia keeps building. I also really liked the setting. The snow and the huge amount of isolation make the whole movie feel trapped. They're stuck together with nowhere to go, which makes the tension even better. The cabin almost feels like its own character. The characters are also just crazy 😭. Pretty much everyone is a terrible person in some way, so you don't really know who to root for. Like the movie says, “No one’s gonna be leaving this place alive.” At that point, you already know things are about to go completely off the rails. Overall, The Hateful Eight is definitely a slow burn, but once it gets going, it's really entertaining. The dialogue, characters, setting, and mystery all work together really well. It's definitely worth watching if you're into Tarantino movies.

I love how you can run his movies back and enjoy them just as much, if not more, the second time, but with this one I don't think I'll be compelled to return to it as much, largely because it's just a weaker, far more self-indulgent and dialogue-heavy movie than most of his other films, but all the characters are pretty much awful people (except Zoe Bell's minor character, love her), so there's not really anyone to root for in the movie. I don't know, I did really enjoy The Hateful 8 but it's definitely his least compelling film. I loved the wintry cinematography and remote cabin setting, and the variation of characters and performances, especially Walton Goggins and Jennifer Jason Leigh, but while it is quite enjoyable and a perfectly good western, it's Tarantino's least serious and worst movie.

This was my third to last Tarantino movie, and I was honestly surprised to still see him pulling out new tricks. It felt like Reservoir Dogs if I had dosed peyote before watching. The Hateful Eight was the complete opposite from the movie I was expecting, being the most cynical spaghetti western which revels in its simplicity and is a character piece through and through. I was pleased to find that, despite the runtime and despite the minimalistic approach, I was never bored. This is one of, if not Tarantino’s funniest movie, with some of his best dialogue. It has a really strong cast in general, but the three that shone the most for me was the master manipulator Major Warren, the oblivious Sheriff Mannix, and the feral opportunist Daisy Domergue. The catalyst of the conflict being a pot of coffee that sends a chain reaction of madness and killing is true Tarantino fashion. If I had to pull away one complaint, it would be that it’s a little too straightforward for its own good. While Reservoir Dogs actively had me pulling my hair out trying to connect the dots, here there was a mix of scenes I found predictable, and scenes that threw me for a loop. But then again, maybe that’s the point. Either way I found more enjoyment in the whacky characters and slapstick brutality than the whodunnit aspect.

Wow. This was an incredible movie. I loved the plot line, the fascinating concept, and the score of the movie. One of the movie's strongest points I feel was the style in which it was filmed. That old-western style and set design, along with the specifics of the camera made it hard to tell this was a film made in 2015, and it works impeccably for the style and immersion into their world. Each character was interesting and captivating, with exceptional performances from each of the ensemble allowing me to want to be invested in each character. The final two chapters are particularly compelling as we see the amazing reveal that really showcases Tarantino as an expert in storytelling. Jennifer Jason Leigh had a career-defining performance, similarly to Walton Goggins going above and beyond as Sheriff. All around an absolutely incredible movie.
